title: Parts of Speech
tagline: Year 1 Foundation — Nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections

introduction.overview: Every word in an English sentence does a job. Grammar groups these jobs into eight classes called parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection. Knowing the part of speech of a word tells you how it can be used, what it can be joined to, and how it changes form. Many grammar questions in placement tests (error spotting, sentence improvement, fill in the blanks) depend on this skill.
introduction.placementRelevance: Parts of speech are the base of the verbal ability section in company aptitude rounds. They are rarely asked in isolation but are needed in almost every grammar question.
introduction.realWorldContext: Spell-checkers, search engines and translation tools all tag every word with its part of speech before doing anything else, and so does every good writer when editing a sentence.

learningObjectives: Define and recognise the eight parts of speech
Decide the part of speech from the job the word does in a sentence
Recognise words that change class between sentences (run, light, round)
Choose the correct case of a pronoun (I/me/my, he/him/his)

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A sentence needs at least a subject and a verb. The subject is who or what the sentence is about; the verb tells what the subject does or is.

coreDefinitions: Noun: a word that names a person, place, thing, animal or idea (Ravi, Chennai, table, honesty). Kinds: common, proper, collective (flock, team), abstract (honesty), material (gold).
Pronoun: a word used in place of a noun (he, she, it, they, who, this, mine).
Verb: a word that shows action, state or being (run, is, seem, have).
Adjective: a word that describes or limits a noun or pronoun (tall boy, three books).
Adverb: a word that tells how, when, where or to what extent about a verb, adjective or another adverb (quickly, very, here).

Preposition: a word that shows the relation of a noun or pronoun to another word (in, on, under, with). Conjunction: a word that joins words, phrases or clauses (and, but, because, although). Interjection: a word that expresses sudden feeling (Hurrah! Alas!).
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: You cannot tell the part of speech of a word by looking at it alone; you must see what it does in the sentence. "Run" is a verb in "I run daily" and a noun in "He went for a run". The question to ask is always: what job is this word doing here?
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Use short tests. Can you put "the" or "a" before it? Then it acts as a noun. Can it take "-ed" or change for tense? It is a verb. Does it describe a noun? It is an adjective. Does it tell how or when the action happened? It is an adverb.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Noun test
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: If the word names something, check whether it can follow an article.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: the honesty of Ravi → honesty is a noun

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Adjective versus adverb
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Adjective → modifies a noun;  Adverb → modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Many adverbs end in -ly, but friendly, lovely and lonely are adjectives.
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: She is a quick learner (adj); She learns quickly (adv)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Pronoun cases
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Subject: I, he, she, we, they, who.  Object: me, him, her, us, them, whom.  Possessive: my, his, her, our, their, whose
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Use the subject form before a verb and the object form after a verb or preposition.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Same word, different class
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: The job in the sentence decides the class
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Run, light, round, after, before can change class.
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Questions that ask "the word X is a ...".
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: after she reached → conjunction; after the meeting → preposition

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Preposition test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: It is followed by a noun or pronoun (its object)
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: If a clause follows, the word is a conjunction.

mainNarrative: Start with the nouns and verbs, since every sentence has at least one of each. In "Ravi reads a book", Ravi and book are nouns and reads is a verb. The article a is a kind of adjective (a determiner) that points to the noun book.

Adjectives and adverbs are the main source of confusion. An adjective answers "which one" or "what kind" about a noun: a quick reply. An adverb answers "how", "when", "where" or "to what extent" about a verb, adjective or adverb: he replied quickly; she is very kind. Words like friendly, lovely and lonely look like adverbs because they end in -ly but they are adjectives.

Pronouns replace nouns and change form with their role. Use "I", "he", "she", "we" and "they" as subjects; use "me", "him", "her", "us" and "them" as objects. After a preposition always use the object form: between you and me, with them, for her.

Prepositions and conjunctions can look alike. After is a preposition when followed by a noun phrase (after the meeting) and a conjunction when followed by a full clause (after she reached home). The test is what follows the word.

Many words move between classes. "A run" is a noun and "to run" is a verb. "The poor need help" uses poor (normally an adjective) as a noun meaning poor people. Always decide the class from the sentence, not from memory.

deepDiveAspects.title: Kinds of nouns worth knowing
deepDiveAspects.content: Collective nouns name a group (a flock of birds, a team of players). Abstract nouns name qualities or ideas (honesty, freedom). Uncountable (mass) nouns such as water, information and advice have no plural form and take no "a".

deepDiveAspects.title: Possessive adjectives and pronouns
deepDiveAspects.content: My, your, his, her, its, our and their come before a noun (my book) and are called possessive adjectives. Mine, yours, his, hers, ours and theirs stand alone (the book is mine) and are possessive pronouns.

problemVariations.description: Name the class of a word in a sentence.
problemVariations.exampleSnippet: In "She sings beautifully", beautifully is an adverb.

solvedExamples.title: Identifying parts of speech
solvedExamples.question: Name the part of speech of each underlined word: "The tall boy quickly ran to the market and bought mangoes."  (tall, quickly, to, and)
givenInfo: Sentence: The tall boy quickly ran to the market and bought mangoes.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Ask what job each word does.

steps.title: tall
steps.explanation: It describes the noun boy, so it is an adjective.

steps.title: quickly
steps.explanation: It tells how the boy ran, so it is an adverb.

steps.title: to
steps.explanation: It shows the relation between ran and market, so it is a preposition.

steps.title: and
steps.explanation: It joins two actions (ran and bought), so it is a conjunction.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: tall – adjective; quickly – adverb; to – preposition; and – conjunction
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Each word is classified by the job it does in the sentence.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Calling "quickly" an adjective because it describes something.

solvedExamples.title: Same word, different class
solvedExamples.question: State the part of speech of "after" in (a) "He left after the meeting." and (b) "She called me after she reached home."
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: A preposition takes a noun; a conjunction joins clauses.

steps.title: Sentence (a)
steps.explanation: After is followed by the noun phrase "the meeting" (no verb), so it is a preposition.

steps.title: Sentence (b)
steps.explanation: After is followed by the clause "she reached home" (subject and verb), so it is a conjunction.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: What follows the word decides its class.

solvedExamples.title: Pronoun case
solvedExamples.question: Choose the correct pronoun: "Between you and ___, the plan is risky."  (I / me / myself / mine)
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: After a preposition, use the object form.

steps.title: Find the structure
steps.explanation: "Between" is a preposition, and "you and ___" is its object.

steps.title: Choose the object form
steps.explanation: The object form of I is me.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: "Between you and me" is correct because both pronouns are objects of the preposition.
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing "I" because "you and I" sounds more polite.

shortcutMethods.title: Job-in-the-sentence test

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Memorise lists of words under each part of speech.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Ask: what does the word do here? Names a thing → noun; replaces a noun → pronoun; shows action or state → verb; describes a noun → adjective; describes a verb/adjective/adverb → adverb; links a noun to another word → preposition; joins clauses → conjunction; shows emotion → interjection.

rulesForApplication: Not every -ly word is an adverb (friendly, lovely, lonely are adjectives).
Pronouns after prepositions take the object form.
If a full clause follows the word, it is a conjunction, not a preposition.
Uncountable nouns such as information and advice take no "a" and no plural "s".

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Assuming the ending decides the class.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check what the word describes: a noun means an adjective.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a subject pronoun after a preposition
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Saying "between you and I" because it sounds formal.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: After a preposition, always use the object form (me, him, her, us, them).

commonMistakes.mistake: Classifying a word out of context
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Thinking that "run" is only a verb.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Decide the class from the sentence every time.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: In a fill-in-the-blank, first decide which part of speech is needed in that gap and discard options of any other class.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Parts of speech form the foundation; spend time here and the later grammar topics become easier.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Error-spotting questions often hinge on an adjective used for an adverb or a wrong pronoun case.

summaryBullets: Eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.
The job in the sentence decides the class.
Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and adverbs.
After a preposition use the object pronoun.
quickFormulas: Subject: I, he, she, we, they
Object: me, him, her, us, them
Possessive: my, his, her, our, their

selfCheckQuestions: Can I name the part of speech of each word in a simple sentence?
Can I give an example of a word used both as a noun and a verb?
Can I choose between "I" and "me" in a compound phrase?
